chunks: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated, from 'Uthman, from Ibn Muskan, from Abu Basir, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
«When a man kisses a woman out of desire, or touches her private part, he must renew the wudu.»

This is interpreted as recommended (mustahabb), or as meaning that he should wash his hand — for washing the hand is sometimes called 'wudu,' as has been previously mentioned — and [the following narration] points to this interpretation.

key_terms.التَّأْوِيلِ: interpretation (ta'wil) — the juristic hermeneutic by which al-Tusi reconciles narrations that appear to contradict the dominant ruling
key_terms.الِاسْتِحْبَابِ: recommendation (mustahabb) — a juristic category for acts that are desirable but not obligatory; al-Tusi's primary hermeneutical tool for harmonising apparently conflicting narrations
key_terms.الْوُضُوءَ: wudu — the ritual ablution prerequisite for salat; the central ruling under discussion
key_terms.شَهْوَةٍ: desire/lust (shahwa) — the qualifying condition specified in the hadith governing when the ruling applies

ai.seo_question: Does kissing a woman out of desire or touching her private part invalidate wudu according to a hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) in Tahdhib al-Ahkam, and how does Sheikh al-Tusi interpret it?
ai.summary: This hadith, attributed to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), states that kissing a woman out of desire or touching her private part requires renewing wudu. Sheikh al-Tusi (author of Tahdhib al-Ahkam) reconciles this with the mainstream Shia ruling that such acts do not invalidate wudu by interpreting the command either as mustahabb (recommended, not obligatory) or as referring merely to washing the hand — a practice that is itself sometimes termed 'wudu' in the transmitted literature.
